title: Remove Letter To Equalize Frequency
description:
# Remove Letter To Equalize Frequency

You are given a lowercase English string `word`.

You must remove **exactly one** character from `word`. After the removal, look only at letters that still appear in the remaining string. Return `true` if all of those remaining letters have the same frequency; otherwise return `false`.

Notes:

* Removing nothing is not allowed.
* Removing one occurrence of a letter is different from deleting every occurrence of that letter.
* A remaining string with only one distinct letter is valid because all present letters have the same frequency.

## Example 1

**Input:** word = "abcc"
**Output:** true
**Explanation:** Remove one `c`; the remaining string is `abc`, and every present letter appears once.

## Example 2

**Input:** word = "aazz"
**Output:** false
**Explanation:** Removing one `a` gives counts `a:1, z:2`; removing one `z` gives counts `a:2, z:1`. Neither result has equal positive frequencies.

## Constraints

* `2 <= word.length <= 100`
* `word` contains only lowercase English letters.

solutions.name: Try Each Letter Type Removal
solutions.description:
## Approach

Count the 26 letter frequencies. For each letter type that appears, temporarily remove one occurrence, then check whether all remaining positive frequencies are equal.

## Key Insight

Only the frequency table matters, not the positions. Trying each letter type is enough because removing any occurrence of the same letter produces the same remaining frequency table.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n + 26*26)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Frequency Distribution Cases
solutions.description:
## Approach

Build the frequency table, then summarize how many letters have each positive frequency. A valid removal has only a few possible shapes: one low-frequency letter disappears, one high-frequency letter drops by one, or there is only one distinct letter.

## Key Insight

After exactly one removal, all positive frequencies must be equal. Therefore the original positive frequencies can contain at most two different values, and one of those values must be repairable by a single decrement.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n + 26)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Sorted Positive Frequencies
solutions.description:
## Approach

Collect only the positive letter frequencies into a list and sort it. Then check the two sorted patterns that one removal can fix: the smallest frequency is a single `1`, or the largest frequency is exactly one above all the others.

## Key Insight

Sorting turns the case analysis into comparisons against the first, second, second-last, and last counts. This is often easier to reason about than maintaining named frequency buckets.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n + 26 log 26)
- Space Complexity: O(26)

solutions.name: Remove Each Index Brute Force
solutions.description:
## Approach

Try deleting every concrete index. For each deletion, rebuild the frequency table of the remaining string and check whether all positive frequencies are equal.

## Key Insight

This route mirrors the prompt most literally and is useful as a correctness baseline. It also prevents confusing "remove one occurrence" with "remove all copies of a letter."

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n * (n + 26))
- Space Complexity: O(1)
